title: Building STARFALL with Claude + ChatGPT taught us that passing tests doesn't mean the combat feels good
author: Correct-Special8912
selftext: We're making STARFALL: Salvage Protocol, an in-development HTML5 space shooter. I'm directing the gameplay and using Claude, ChatGPT, Blender and a local coordination workspace to help implement, test and iterate. It's not released or being [sold.One](http://sold.One) lesson from actual playtests: AI-assisted iteration made it easy to add enemy types, boss attacks and UI telegraphs. Soon we had so many targeting lines and oversized attack circles that the indicators hid the explosions and ships they were meant to clarify. A feature can be technically correct and still make combat worse.We're now separating automated checks from manual feel tests. Our scripts catch loading, progression and upgrade regressions. Actual gameplay captures expose different problems: steering sensitivity, collision feedback, attack readability and whether a boss feels distinct. Our salvage/research loop lets the player reverse-engineer boss technology, but that has to be fun in the real browser build, not just impressive in a feature list.We recently captured genuine first-fleet, boss-fight and station-research screenshots for the devlog: [https://www.indiedb.com/games/starfall-salvage-protocol/imagesHow](https://www.indiedb.com/games/starfall-salvage-protocol/imagesHow) are other AI-assisted game developers keeping automated feature output from outpacing hands-on playtesting? Do you keep a separate candidate build while experimenting with new agents/assets?

comments.author: Captain_Slib
comments.body: I'd love to hear more about your feel tests. How are you determining what feels good vs what doesnt?

replies.author: Correct-Special8912
replies.body: We don't have a single "fun score" — we're judging a few repeatable things in hands-on runs: can I steer and track a target without overshooting, can I understand a boss warning while all the effects are firing, and does a salvage upgrade actually change the next fight? We replay encounters and watch the captured footage, especially moments where a hit feels unfair or the HUD hides the threat. Automated tests tell us the systems function; they don't tell us whether steering or combat feels satisfying. We're still refining that process. Do you use a formal playtest rubric, or mostly compare before/after builds?

comments.author: PocketStudio
comments.body: What worked for me: make the automated run count what the player actually sees, not just that the logic passed. My 150-run sweep answered the game's event prompts through code, so it passed while one whole event type never reached the screen. I only found that by playing a season by hand. Now the checks log "shown on screen" counts (0 = fail), and every new mechanic gets a short manual play before I trust the bots.

replies.author: Correct-Special8912
replies.body: That's a really useful distinction: an event firing in code doesn't mean the player ever saw it. We've had a similar gap between passing automated checks and what the browser footage actually showed. The idea of failing a run when an expected onscreen event count is zero is a strong QA gate, especially for boss arrivals and attack warnings. I'm going to bring that into our next QA review alongside the short manual runs. Thanks for sharing the concrete 150-run example — much more actionable than just 'test more'.
